Interface RigidPhysicsAPI

All Known Implementing Classes:
RigidPhysicsApiImpl
public interface RigidPhysicsAPI
The single entry point to GTRigidPhysics.

Getting hold of it

Either route works — pick one: 
// Route A: static accessor (least ceremony)
RigidPhysicsAPI api = RigidPhysicsProvider.get();

// Route B: Bukkit services manager (when you would rather not touch Provider at compile time)
RegisteredServiceProvider<RigidPhysicsAPI> rsp =
        Bukkit.getServicesManager().getRegistration(RigidPhysicsAPI.class);
RigidPhysicsAPI api = rsp == null ? null : rsp.getProvider();

When to get it

Not from your plugin's onLoad() — GTRigidPhysics has not been enabled at that point, so you are guaranteed to get nothing. The right moment is your own onEnable(), with the dependency declared in paper-plugin.yml so the load order is actually guaranteed: 
dependencies:
  server:
    GTRigidPhysics:
      load: BEFORE
      required: true    # use false for a soft dependency — and remember to null-check

On "the service may not exist"

Even once the plugin itself is enabled, the physics runtime may still be unavailable — for instance when the server runs on an unsupported platform (this plugin needs Windows x86-64 / Linux x86-64 / Linux aarch64), or when the native library fails to load. In those cases the plugin disables itself and this interface is never registered. So null-checking when you obtain the service is mandatory, not defensive-coding fastidiousness.

One level finer: while isPhysicsAvailable() is false, calls into the sub-services do not throw — they silently do nothing (spawns return null, forces return 0). Check that method when you need to tell "the plugin is not installed" apart from "it is installed but physics did not come up".

Threading

Unless a method's own documentation says otherwise, every method on this API must be called from the server main thread. Dispatching onto the internal Jolt physics thread is the implementation's responsibility; callers neither need to nor should do it themselves.

  • Method Details

    • apiVersion

      @NotNull @NotNull String apiVersion()
      The API contract version, such as "1.0.0", following semantic versioning.

      This value tracks the api module and evolves independently of the plugin implementation version: when the implementation ships 1.0.3 to fix a bug, the API version stays 1.0.0 — because the contract did not change. If your plugin has a hard requirement on some newly added capability, compare against this value rather than implementationVersion().

      Returns:
      the API contract version
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • implementationVersion

      @NotNull @NotNull String implementationVersion()
      The plugin implementation version — that is, the version of the jar actually installed on the server.

      For logging and diagnostics only. Do not make capability decisions from it.

      Returns:
      the plugin implementation version
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • isPhysicsAvailable

      boolean isPhysicsAvailable()
      Whether the physics runtime is actually available.

      Typical reasons for false: the server CPU architecture is unsupported, the native library failed to load, or the physics thread has stopped after a fatal error. The sub-services remain safe to call in that state — they simply have no effect.

      Returns:
      true once the native physics runtime is ready
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • structure

      @NotNull @NotNull StructuralIntegrityService structure()
      Load-bearing structure service: evaluate structural integrity, query weak points, and annotate region templates.

      The split against collapses() is "look" versus "do": the collapse service makes a building fall, this one tells you whether it would without changing the world (region annotation aside). Use it for structure scanners, AI target selection, and level acceptance checks.

      Returns:
      the structural integrity service, never null
      Since:
      1.1.0

    • settle

      @NotNull @NotNull SettleService settle()
      Settle rule service: once debris comes to rest, does it become a real block, a dropped item, or nothing at all.

      The division of labour against collapses() is "process" versus "result": the collapse service brings the building down, this one decides what is left on the ground afterwards. Without it the whole physics layer is just a visual effect and the terrain comes out untouched.

      Besides queries it also allows rules to be overridden at runtime — this is meant for ephemeral worlds: an arena is recreated every round with a UUID in its name, so a server owner has no way to write it into settle.yml.

      Returns:
      the settle rule service, never null
      Since:
      1.2.0

    • debris

      @NotNull @NotNull ExplosionDebrisService debris()
      Explosion debris service: turn blocks destroyed outright by an explosion into scattering physics debris.

      How this differs from collapses(): collapse handles the blocks that lost their support, debris handles the blocks that were blown apart — which in vanilla simply vanish. This service sends them flying instead.

      Returns:
      the explosion debris service, never null
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • cameraEffects

      @NotNull @NotNull Optional<CameraEffectService> cameraEffects()
      Camera effect service: the screen roll and shake caused by explosions and collapses.

      This returns an Optional rather than a nullable value because the feature can be switched off wholesale by the server owner (enabled: false in camera-roll.yml). When it is off the service is never constructed, so the steady-state cost is genuinely zero. That is a different situation from "physics is unavailable", and the type makes the difference explicit.

      Returns:
      the camera effect service, or Optional.empty() when the feature is disabled
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • vehicles

      @NotNull @NotNull VehicleService vehicles()
      Real physics vehicle service: spawn handles for wheeled vehicles, manual driving input, and the built-in "look to steer" player driving mode.

      Vehicles are driven by jolt-jni's VehicleConstraint — four independently suspended wheels plus engine, transmission and differential. This is fundamentally different from fake driving that nudges a rigid body with an impulse every tick.

      Returns:
      the vehicle service, never null
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • mechanisms

      @NotNull @NotNull MechanismService mechanisms()
      Mechanism service: the motor control entry point for rigid bodies driven by hinge or slider constraints (windmills, revolving doors, pistons).

      Mechanisms are driven by the same constraint machinery as VehicleConstraint: a hinge (HingeConstraint) restricts a body to rotation about one axis, a slider (SliderConstraint) restricts it to translation along one axis, both with position and velocity motors.

      Returns:
      the mechanism service, never null
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • characters

      @NotNull @NotNull CharacterService characters()
      Virtual character service: characters that move through the physics world and are blocked by terrain and rigid bodies.

      Characters are driven by jolt-jni's CharacterVirtual — a kinematic capsule that does not consume rigid body budget, walks along the ground, climbs steps, and is blocked by dice and vehicles. A good foundation for NPCs that interact with the physics world.

      Returns:
      the character service, never null
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • ragdolls

      @NotNull @NotNull RagdollService ragdolls()
      Ragdoll service: seven-part rigid body humanoid skeletons that collapse in the physics world.

      Ragdolls are driven by jolt-jni's Ragdoll — head, torso, two arms and two legs are each a dynamic rigid body, joined into a skeleton by SwingTwist constraints, falling under gravity and scatterable by a shove. A good foundation for "NPC drops dead" animations.

      Returns:
      the ragdoll service, never null
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • interaction

      @NotNull @NotNull InteractionService interaction()
      Rigid body interaction service: grab, release, throw and freeze — the foundation for physics guns and wands.

      Use it together with PhysicsBodyService.raycast(Location, Vector, double): pick the body in front of the crosshair with a ray, then grab, hover and throw it through this service. Grabbing is a stateful interaction; the state machine lives in the main plugin.

      Returns:
      the interaction service, never null
      Since:
      1.0.0

    • systems

      @NotNull @NotNull SystemSettingsService systems()
      Per-system toggles: query and switch the enabled state of each feature system (collapse, explosion debris, standalone objects, impact consequences, TNT and so on). All are enabled by default.

      The "system management" page of the panel addon is built on this — it lists every system, toggles on click, takes effect immediately and persists to systems.yml.

      Returns:
      the system settings service, never null
      Since:
      1.1.0
